analysis_trace.content: Single-blind RCT of EMG-triggered electrical stimulation vs conventional physiotherapy for median/ulnar nerve repair. N=26, 2 parallel arms, NOT_YET_RECRUITING, expected completion 2027-11-30. Primary: Manual muscle test at 12/24 weeks. Secondary: Grip strength (kg) and Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire at 12/24 weeks.
Peripheral nerve injuries (median/ulnar nerve repair). Post-surgical rehabilitation to improve motor function of wrist/finger extensors (EDC, ECRL/B, ECU).

Adults 18-65 years with intact communication, no prior neurological/orthopedic diseases affecting extremity. Excludes CNS involvement, pregnancy, pacemakers, arrhythmias, epilepsy. Small sample (n=26 estimated).

EMG-triggered FES: patient-initiated stimulation via surface electrodes at 60Hz, 300µs pulse width, requiring active cognitive participation. Enhances motor learning through contingent feedback and neuroplasticity. Targets extensor muscles (EDC, ECRL/B, ECU) for functional recovery.

Primary-0: Manual muscle test (MMT) - ordinal scale 0-5, assesses muscle strength. Secondary-0: Grip strength dynamometry/pinch gauge (kg) - continuous measure. Secondary-1: MHQ - patient-reported hand function 0-100 (higher=better except pain). All measured at 12 and 24 weeks post-surgery.

Retrieved Europe PMC records on electrical stimulation for nerve regeneration (PMID:36908597, 35317464), neuromuscular ES systematic reviews, EMG-triggered FES case reports. No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered FES in median/ulnar nerve repair. Indirect evidence from stroke rehabilitation shows EMG-triggered FES improves motor function. Peripheral nerve repair recovery typically shows gradual motor improvement over 12-24 weeks.

PMID:35317464 (systematic review ES in peripheral nerve regeneration): evidence_role=indirect_direction, mismatch_reason=different ES modality (not EMG-triggered), numeric_use_allowed=false. PMID:36908597 (ES therapy for peripheral nerve injury): evidence_role=indirect_direction, mismatch_reason=general ES not EMG-triggered specific, numeric_use_allowed=false. PMID:40309882 (EMG-triggered FES for facial palsy): evidence_role=mechanism_background, mismatch_reason=stroke not nerve repair, numeric_use_allowed=false. PMID:41154169 (EMG-triggered ES topography): evidence_role=mechanism_background, mismatch_reason=healthy adults not nerve injury, numeric_use_allowed=false.

EMG-triggered FES has mechanistic rationale for motor recovery via neuroplasticity and contingent feedback. Conventional physiotherapy alone provides standard care. Expected effect: EMG-FES group shows modest improvement over conventional group in muscle strength, grip strength, and hand function at 12 and 24 weeks. Small sample size limits statistical power. No direct numerical anchor available.
Surface electrode ES generally safe. Exclusion criteria address pacemaker/arrhythmia risks. No serious safety signals expected beyond mild skin irritation or discomfort from stimulation.

1) Small sample (n=26) may limit power to detect clinically meaningful differences. 2) NOT_YET_RECRUITING status introduces enrollment/timeline risk. 3) Single-blind design may have assessor bias despite masking. 4) No prior RCT evidence for this specific intervention in nerve repair. 5) Heterogeneity in nerve injury severity/repair quality may confound outcomes.

No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered FES in median/ulnar nerve repair. No published effect sizes for this specific population. Reliance on indirect evidence from stroke and general peripheral nerve rehabilitation.

analysis_trace.content: Single-blind RCT of EMG-triggered electrical stimulation vs conventional physiotherapy for median/ulnar nerve repair. N=26, 2 parallel arms, NOT_YET_RECRUITING, expected completion 2027-11-30. Primary: Manual muscle test at 12/24 weeks. Secondary: Grip strength (kg) and Michigan Hand Outcomes Questionnaire at 12/24 weeks.
Peripheral nerve injuries (median/ulnar nerve repair). Post-surgical rehabilitation to improve motor function of wrist/finger extensors (EDC, ECRL/B, ECU).

Adults 18-65 years with intact communication, no prior neurological/orthopedic diseases affecting extremity. Excludes CNS involvement, pregnancy, pacemakers, arrhythmias, epilepsy. Small sample (n=26 estimated).

EMG-triggered FES: patient-initiated stimulation via surface electrodes at 60Hz, 300µs pulse width, requiring active cognitive participation. Enhances motor learning through contingent feedback and neuroplasticity. Targets extensor muscles (EDC, ECRL/B, ECU) for functional recovery.

Primary-0: Manual muscle test (MMT) - ordinal scale 0-5, assesses muscle strength. Secondary-0: Grip strength dynamometry/pinch gauge (kg) - continuous measure. Secondary-1: MHQ - patient-reported hand function 0-100 (higher=better except pain). All measured at 12 and 24 weeks post-surgery.

Retrieved Europe PMC records on electrical stimulation for nerve regeneration (PMID:36908597, 35317464), neuromuscular ES systematic reviews, EMG-triggered FES case reports. No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered FES in median/ulnar nerve repair. Indirect evidence from stroke rehabilitation shows EMG-triggered FES improves motor function. Peripheral nerve repair recovery typically shows gradual motor improvement over 12-24 weeks.

PMID:35317464 (systematic review ES in peripheral nerve regeneration): evidence_role=indirect_direction, mismatch_reason=different ES modality (not EMG-triggered), numeric_use_allowed=false. PMID:36908597 (ES therapy for peripheral nerve injury): evidence_role=indirect_direction, mismatch_reason=general ES not EMG-triggered specific, numeric_use_allowed=false. PMID:40309882 (EMG-triggered FES for facial palsy): evidence_role=mechanism_background, mismatch_reason=stroke not nerve repair, numeric_use_allowed=false. PMID:41154169 (EMG-triggered ES topography): evidence_role=mechanism_background, mismatch_reason=healthy adults not nerve injury, numeric_use_allowed=false.

EMG-triggered FES has mechanistic rationale for motor recovery via neuroplasticity and contingent feedback. Conventional physiotherapy alone provides standard care. Expected effect: EMG-FES group shows modest improvement over conventional group in muscle strength, grip strength, and hand function at 12 and 24 weeks. Small sample size limits statistical power. No direct numerical anchor available.
Surface electrode ES generally safe. Exclusion criteria address pacemaker/arrhythmia risks. No serious safety signals expected beyond mild skin irritation or discomfort from stimulation.

1) Small sample (n=26) may limit power to detect clinically meaningful differences. 2) NOT_YET_RECRUITING status introduces enrollment/timeline risk. 3) Single-blind design may have assessor bias despite masking. 4) No prior RCT evidence for this specific intervention in nerve repair. 5) Heterogeneity in nerve injury severity/repair quality may confound outcomes.

No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered FES in median/ulnar nerve repair. No published effect sizes for this specific population. Reliance on indirect evidence from stroke and general peripheral nerve rehabilitation.

analysis_trace: Trial Identification: NCT07532499 is a single-blind, randomized controlled study investigating EMG-triggered electrical stimulation plus conventional physiotherapy versus conventional physiotherapy alone after median/ulnar nerve repair. Status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING. Expected completion: 2027-11-30.

Patient Population: Adults aged 18-65 with peripheral nerve injuries (median/ulnar nerve), post-surgical repair. Exclusion criteria include CNS involvement, pregnancy, cardiac pacemakers/arrhythmias, epilepsy. Sample size: 26 estimated.

Target Mechanism: EMG-triggered electrical stimulation targets extensor muscles (EDC, ECRL/B, ECU) to restore muscle weakness from immobilization. Stimulation parameters: 60 Hz, 300 µS pulse width, 0.5s ramp, 10s contraction/30s rest cycle, 12 sessions over 4 weeks starting week 5 post-surgery.

Evidence Sources Retrieved: (1) ClinicalTrials.gov protocol NCT07532499 - trial design only; (2) PMC9028466 - EMG-triggered multichannel FES in stroke patients showing higher gains in FMA-AS vs cNMES; (3) Frontiers in Neurology 2023 review on ES for PNI - clinical studies show ES enhances axon growth and sensorimotor recovery; (4) PMC11962904 - systematic review showing motor outcomes (MMT) most frequently reported after PNI; (5) PMC3746316 - review on peripheral nerve surgery outcomes including MMT, grip/pinch strength, MHQ.

Evidence Role Assessment: PMC9028466 - indirect_direction (stroke vs nerve repair, different pathology but EMG-triggered ES mechanism similar); Frontiers review - indirect_direction (general ES efficacy for PNI); PMC11962904 - mechanism_background (outcome measurement patterns); PMC3746316 - indirect_direction (outcome tools for nerve repair). No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered ES specifically in median/ulnar nerve repair.

Endpoint Interpretation - primary-0 (Manual muscle test): MMT is standard for motor recovery assessment after nerve repair. Evidence suggests ES can enhance motor recovery. Predict EMG+PT group shows greater improvement than PT alone at 12 and 24 weeks. Effect size moderate based on stroke literature extrapolation.

Endpoint Interpretation - secondary-0 (Grip/pinch strength): Dynamometry is objective measure of functional recovery. ES may reduce muscle atrophy and improve reinnervation. Predict EMG+PT group shows 15-25% greater strength recovery vs PT alone.

Endpoint Interpretation - secondary-1 (MHQ): Patient-reported outcome for hand function. Domains include function, ADL, pain, work, aesthetics, satisfaction. Predict EMG+PT group shows clinically meaningful improvement in function and ADL domains; pain domain may show mixed results.

Key Uncertainties: (1) Trial not yet recruiting - no actual outcome data exists; (2) Small sample size (n=26) limits statistical power; (3) Extrapolation from stroke and general PNI literature to specific median/ulnar nerve repair population; (4) Optimal ES parameters not established for this specific indication; (5) Timing of intervention (week 5) relative to nerve regeneration biology.

Safety Analysis: ES generally safe for peripheral nerve rehabilitation. Contraindications (pacemakers, epilepsy) excluded. Expected adverse events: mild skin irritation, discomfort. No serious safety signals anticipated.

Evidence-to-Prediction: Based on mechanistic rationale (ES promotes nerve regeneration, reduces muscle atrophy) and indirect evidence from related populations, EMG-triggered ES is predicted to provide additional benefit over conventional physiotherapy alone for motor recovery outcomes.

Coverage Gaps: No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered ES in median/ulnar nerve repair; no published results from this specific trial; limited data on optimal stimulation protocols; no long-term follow-up data available.

PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC9028466 PMID: 35455881 Abstract This preliminary randomized clinical trial explores the efficacy of task-oriented electromyography (EMG)-triggered multichannel functional electrical stimulation (EMG-MES) compared to single-channel cyclic neuromuscular electrical stimulation (cNMES) on regaining control of voluntary movements (CVM) and the ability to execute arm-hand-activities in subacute stroke patients with moderate arm paresis. Twelve ischemic stroke patients (Fugl-Meyer Assessment Arm Section (FMA-AS) score: 19–47) with comparable demographics were block-randomized to receive 15 sessions of cNMES or EMG-MES over three weeks additionally to a conventional neurorehabilitation program including task-oriented arm training. FMA-AS, Box-and-Block Test (BBT), and Stroke-Impact-Scale (SIS) were recorded at baseline and follow-up. All participants demonstrated significant improvement in FMA-AS and BBT. Participants treated with EMG-MES had a higher mean gain in FMA-AS than those treated with cNMES. In the SIS daily activities domain, both groups improved non-significantly; participants in the EMG-MES group had higher improvement in arm-hand use and stroke recovery. EMG-MES treatment demonstrated a higher gain of CVM and self-reported daily activities, arm-hand use, and stroke recovery compared to cNMES treatment of the wrist only. The protocol of this proof-of-concept study seems robust enough to be used in a larger trial to confirm these preliminary findings. Keywords: moderate arm paresis, subacute stroke, motor recovery, control of voluntary movements, EMG-triggered multichannel electrical stimulation, functional electrical stimulation 1. Introduction Stroke is the main reason for disability in adults [ 1 ]. Neurorehabilitation focuses on regaining control of voluntary movements (CVM) to optimize task performance in activities of daily living, thus improving quality of life. Houwink et al. [ 2 ] found that 78% of stroke patients with an initial CVM in the shoulder and elbow at admission to first in-patient rehabilitation achieved advanced arm and hand capacity after discharge. Recovery of CVM in paretic arm and hand (with or without synkinesis) can best be quantified with the Fugl-Meyer Assessment Arm Section (FMA-AS; score 0–66) [ 3 , 4 ]. In recent years, electrical stimulation (ES) of an upper extremity is demonstrated to be a promising intervention to improve arm and hand function in neurorehabilitation [ 5 , 6 ]. Data have been published on the effects of both cyclical and electromyography (EMG)-triggered single-channel ES [ 6 , 7 , 8 ]. The research exhibits the positive effects of Functional Electrical Stimulation (FES) to improve the ability to perform activities [ 6 , 8 ]. Interventions that support voluntary movements through an ES triggered by an EMG signal, which is induced by a target movement performed from the affected individual, are increasingly gaining acceptance. This type of intervention was described as even more reinforcing than cyclic stimulation due to the proprioceptive feedback and voluntary component involved. Motor improvements in hand function following a stroke have been observed [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ]. A meta-analysis describes the comparison of EMG-triggered ES to conventional therapy and demonstrates improved upper limb impairment in those more than 3-month post stroke. The benefits within the first month and the comparison of the effects of different EMG-stimulation protocols are not clear yet. These authors suggested that EMG-ES leads to greater gains in post stroke upper extremity impairment [ 7 ]. In a study on stroke patients, EMG-ES was compared with classical transcutaneous nerve stimulation (TENS) below the motor threshold. EMG-triggered stimulation leads to better short-term effects in the intervention group [ 13 ]. In contrast to a pure repetition of movement in one joint, functional multi-joint arm-and-hand activities can be elicited by EMG-triggered multichannel stimulation patterns (EMG-MES) [ 11 , 14 , 15 ]. Patients with moderate arm paresis can use their residual CVM to trigger voluntary movements [ 7 , 16 ]. A higher activity level of the patient has been proposed as an additional advantage for this type of intervention. Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, The First Affiliated Hospital, School of Medicine, Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China See more Article metrics View details Abstract Peripheral nerve injury is common and frequently occurs in extremity trauma patients. The motor and sensory impairment caused by the injury will affect patients' daily life and social work. Surgical therapeutic approaches don't assure functional recovery, which may lead to neuronal atrophy and hinder accelerated regeneration. Rehabilitation is a necessary stage for patients to recover better. A meaningful role in non-pharmacological intervention is played by rehabilitation, through individualized electrical stimulation therapy. Clinical studies have shown that electrical stimulation enhances axon growth during nerve repair and accelerates sensorimotor recovery. According to different effects and parameters, electrical stimulation can be divided into neuromuscular, transcutaneous, and functional electrical stimulation. The therapeutic mechanism of electrical stimulation may be to reduce muscle atrophy and promote muscle reinnervation by increasing the expression of structural protective proteins and neurotrophic factors. Meanwhile, it can modulate sensory feedback and reduce neuralgia by inhibiting the descending pathway. However, there are not many summary clinical application parameters of electrical stimulation, and the long-term effectiveness and safety also need to be further explored. This article aims to explore application methodologies for effective electrical stimulation in the rehabilitation of peripheral nerve injury, with simultaneous consideration for fundamental principles of electrical stimulation and the latest technology. The highlight of this paper is to identify the most appropriate stimulation parameters (frequency, intensity, duration) to achieve efficacious electrical stimulation in the rehabilitation of peripheral nerve injury. 1. Introduction The peripheral nervous system, including cranial nerves, spinal nerves, and autonomic nerves, is a nerve trunk, nerve plexus, ganglion, and nerve terminal composed of perikarya and nerve fibers, which mainly connect the peripheral sensory apparatus and the central nervous system. Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is a kind of motor and sensory disorder caused by damage to the structure of peripheral nerves. The incidence of PNI caused by trauma is roughly 5%, including brachial plexus and root injuries ( 1 ). After nerve injury, damaged axons are not able to regenerate completely. Therefore, it is important to provide appropriate therapies to reconnect nerves in the injured area and to accelerate the growth rate of nerve ( 2 ). At present, the treatment methods for nerve injury are mainly divided into surgical treatment and non-surgical treatment ( 3 – 5 ). Electrical stimulation (ES) is the most commonly used non-surgical treatment. Most studies used low-frequency ES to promote nerve regeneration, but the method and frequency range of ES need to be standardized because high-frequency ES will aggravate nerve damage ( 6 ). The standard ES parameter of 20 Hz for one hour immediately after the repair is well known. However, its utility and efficacy for various nerves have never been defined. This review focuses on a framework to develop a new ES paradigm enabling future clinical translation. 2. Peripheral nerve anatomy Peripheral nerves refer to all nerves other than the brain and spinal cord, including ganglia, nerve trunks, nerve plexus and nerve ending. The center of the anatomical structure of the peripheral nerve is the nerve fiber. The endoneurium wraps around the nerve fibers to form the nerve bundle that is surrounded by loose connective tissue. The epineurium then wraps the nerve bundle to form a complete peripheral nerve ( 7 ). There are many pathogenic factors, such as infection, ischemia, trauma, metabolic disorders, poisoning, nutritional deficiency, and iatrogenic injury (such as chemotherapy, radiotherapy, etc.). Peripheral injury can lead to severe dysfunction, often affecting the ability of patients to perform activities of daily living. 3. Classification of peripheral nerve injury Common peripheral nerve injuries include brachial plexus nerve injury, axillary nerve injury, cutaneous nerve injury, median nerve injury, radial nerve injury, ulnar nerve injury, femoral nerve injury, sciatic nerve injury, and common peroneal nerve injury. According to Seddon's classification in 1943, PNI was divided into three types neurapraxia, axonal disruption, and nerve rupture. According to the 1951 Sunderland classification, the PNI was divided into 5 types. Type I: focal demyelination; Type II: damage to axons but endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium intact; Type III damage to axons and endoneurium but perineurium and epineurium intact; Type IV: damage to axons, endoneurium, and perineurium but epineurium intact; Type V: complete loss of continuity ( Figure 1 ). For type IV and V injuries, it is necessary to suture the nerve transection by surgeries, including nerve manipulation and bridging ( 8 ). PMC Copyright notice PMCID: PMC11962904 PMID: 40182860 Abstract Purpose The manner in which outcomes are reported after peripheral nerve injury (PNI) varies tremendously and often centers on surgeon-manual muscle testing. The purpose of our systematic review was to quantify the use of outcome measures after PNI in the contemporary literature (published in 2008 and beyond) and to evaluate which domains of recovery are assessed most frequently. Methods With the assistance of a medical librarian, we performed a systematic review of the literature published in or after 2008 (to represent the last 15 years) for patients with upper-extremity PNI. We excluded articles with <5 participants, minors, brachial plexus or digital nerve injuries, compressive neuropathies, or <6 months of follow-up. Data were extracted to identify which outcome measures were used in each study, categorizing the outcome measures under the domains of motor, sensory, function, and pain. Results Of the 4 outcome domains (pain, motor, sensory, and function), motor was reported the most frequently, followed by function. Within the motor category, more than two-thirds of the studies used manual muscle testing for assessment. Half of the articles reported outcomes in 2 of the 4 assessed domains. Pain was the least assessed domain, reported in 11 of 68 articles. Conclusion While there has been incorporation of functional outcomes, the majority of the literature in the last 15 years remains focused on surgeon-reported muscle testing and does not adequately reflect the multiple domains affected by PNI. Pain is the least frequently reported domain, despite being an issue that frequently vexes PNI patients. Clinical Relevance There is a need for clinicians and researchers to agree upon a common set of outcome measures for PNI that (A) encompass perspectives of clinicians and patients and (B) reflect multiple domains affected by PNI. This will improve the quality of outcome reporting and facilitate future comparative effectiveness studies. Key words: Nerve repair outcomes, Peripheral nerve injury, Upper-extremity nerve injury Peripheral nerve injuries (PNI) present challenges for patients and their health care providers. Despite notable scientific and microsurgical advancements in surgical treatment, optimal outcomes after reconstruction are not achieved consistently. While there are numerous efforts to improve outcomes after PNI, the manner in which outcomes are assessed is not standardized and is widely variable. Rigorous comparative effectiveness research depends on consistency in how outcomes are reported as well as using measures that reflect the multiple domains affected by PNI (such as physical function, pain, sensation, and quality of life). To date, the vast majority of reported outcomes are based on surgeon-reported manual muscle testing using the British Medical Research Council (MRC), which was invented in the post-World War 2 era to categorize the recovery of injured soldiers. 1 , 2 While widely used, the MRC scale is prone to interrater and intrarater variability and only reflects peak strength, rather than fatiguability. 3 MacAvoy and Green 1 reported that the proposed “4/5” strength category according to the MRC guidelines includes 96% of the possible strength in that arm, reflecting the lack of precision in using this measure to assess function rigorously and objectively. In addition, using a single measure to assess outcome does not capture the complete picture of a patient’s function. Assessments of quality of life and satisfaction with outcome are valued by patients with nerve injury, 4 yet are reported rarely in the literature. 5 Keeping in line with a general trend in the surgical literature toward patient-reported outcomes, more recent publications have included a more robust collection of outcomes after PNI. 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 As part of a larger effort to develop a core outcome set for PNI, 13 we conducted a systematic review of the contemporary published literature (defined as articles published in the last 15 years) to determine which outcome measures have been reported recently for PNI. We examined the methods used for outcome measurement and the frequency of specific outcome measures across studies. We hypothesized that while there would be a wide range of outcome measures reported in the contemporary literature, there would be little consistency in which outcomes are used. Methods Information sources Given the nature of this project, we did not seek approval from our institutional review board for this systematic review of the literature. We collaborated with a medical librarian for the literature search. The medical librarian searched the published literature for outcomes after nerve exploration, neurolysis, nerve repair, nerve grafting, or nerve transfer for upper-extremity nerve injuries. The search strategies were established using a combination of standardized terms and keywords and executed in the databases Ovid Medline 1946-, Embase.com 1947-, and Web of Science 1900- on March 12, 2024, using an English-only language filter and a date limit of 1993–current (although only articles published during or after 2008 eventually were included to reflect the contemporary literature of the last 15 years). Conference abstracts and case reports were excluded from the search. A total of 6,084 citations were imported into Covidence; 1,726 duplicates were assumed to be identified accurately and removed for a total of 4,358 unique citations. Full electronic search strategies are provided in the supplementary material . Eligibility criteria To capture how outcome studies have been reported in the contemporary literature, we only included articles published in or after 2008 that reported on surgically-treated upper-extremity PNIs in an adult population and had distinct reported outcome measures. Studies were excluded if they were (1) non-English, abstracts, conference proceedings, letters, perspective pieces, reviews, or editorials; (2) reported on brachial plexus injuries, digital nerve injuries, or compressive neuropathies; (3) did not report at least 6 months of follow-up for each included participant; (4) included any individuals aged <18 years; or (5) had <5 participants in their data population. Published articles that included treatment of lower-extremity nerve injuries did not meet inclusion criteria, as our systematic review focused exclusively on upper-extremity nerve injuries Selection process Three investigators independently screened and reviewed the full texts of returned studies, applying the above inclusion and exclusion criteria and using Covidence systematic review software (Veritas Health Innovation, Melbourne, Australia). Any disagreements between any 2 investigators were resolved by a third investigator; no disagreements were encountered. A κ coefficient was calculated to assess interrater reliability agreement on inclusion. Three investigators then worked independently to group, review, and extract data from each study. A Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) flow diagram for this review is included in the Supplementary Figure 1 and Figure 2 (available on the Journal's website at wwwjhsgo.org ). Data extraction and synthesis For each study, data on specific outcome measurements used were extracted. For each study, the number of participants, type of intervention performed, average length of follow-up, and types of outcomes measured were recorded. In assessing the frequency of outcome measures, we included only outcomes that were reported in >1 article and excluded any that were specific only to a single article. We categorized the selected outcome measures into 4 domains: motor, sensory, function, and pain. We included employment in the domain of function given that the former is a reflection of the latter. Measures of mental health and personality also were included under the domain of function. PRISMA Compliance We followed the 2020 guidelines for the PRISMA for each stage of this systematic review, including the literature search, application of inclusion and exclusion criteria, and data extraction. Results Study selection A full- text review was performed for 211 abstracts of the 4357 unique citations identified. Sixty-eight of the 211 articles evaluating 2,491 patients were selected for inclusion ( Supplementary Table 1 , available on the Journal's website at www.jhsgo.org ). Twenty-three of these studies originated in Asia, 17 in Europe, 12 in North America, 9 in South America, 6 in Africa, and 1 in Australia. All 9 of the South American studies were from Brazil and 9 of 12 North American studies were from the United States. Six studies were from Turkey. The 68 articles included a variety of treatment options including nerve repair, nerve transfer, tendon transfer, and combination procedures. This review makes a list of measurements addressing these aspects as well as advantage and disadvantage of each tool. Because of complexities of neurophysiology, assessment remains a difficult process, which requires researchers focus on measurements best relevant to specific conditions and research questions. Keywords: Peripheral nerve, Hand surgery, Outcomes assessment The outcomes movement, initiated in 1988 was stimulated by the national emphasis on cost containment and efforts to limit geographic differences in the use of various medical procedures. 1 - 3 Goals of the outcomes movement included “increased understanding of the effectiveness of different interventions, the use of this information to make possible better decision making by physicians and patients, and the development of standards to guide physicians and aid third-party payers in optimizing the use of resources, by investigating and comparing patient experiences.” 1 , 4 Patient experiences can range from mortality, physiologic measures, reduction of symptoms, improvement in daily functioning, clinical events, to patient satisfaction. 4 , 5 The outcomes chosen to evaluate care need to be carefully considered based on criteria that are most pertinent to the patient’s need. Additionally vital are the criteria for selecting outcome measurement instruments, which comprise of reliability, validity, and responsiveness of measures, their clinical utility, and relationship to the care under investigation. 5 Peripheral nerve injuries can be caused by trauma, accidental injuries during extensive surgery, nerve tumors, compressive disease or congenital anomalies, with the majority (81%) located on upper extremity. 6 , 7 Among upper or lower-limb trauma, incidence of nerve injuries is reported to be 1.64%, with crush injuries having the highest rate at 1.9%. 8 These injuries may lead to irreversible disabilities in patients, such as sensory loss, deficient motor function, pain problems in terms of cold intolerance and hyperesthesia, that ultimately impair hand function, and affect quality of life at work and in society. 7 Despite marked advances in the neuroscience arena, peripheral nerve injuries continue to pose challenges for surgical reconstruction, as the clinical outcomes still appear unsatisfactory. 6 , 7 Advances in this field will require accurate measures of treatment effectiveness to assess new treatments that are certainly on the horizon. The assessment of recovery after peripheral nerve surgery remains a challenging process to therapists and surgeons. Numerous cellular and biochemical mechanisms that occur in peripheral and central nervous systems affect the outcomes and result in difficult evaluation of recovery. 9 Measurement instruments for peripheral nerve surgery need to aid clinical diagnosis, assess and compare surgical repair techniques, track rehabilitation progress, provide feedback to both patient and therapist, as well as ascertain disability after injury. 9 The list of objectives useful in evaluation of hand function after peripheral nerve repair is provided in Table 1 . analysis_trace: Trial Identification: NCT07532499 is a single-blind, randomized controlled study investigating EMG-triggered electrical stimulation plus conventional physiotherapy versus conventional physiotherapy alone after median/ulnar nerve repair. Status: NOT_YET_RECRUITING. Expected completion: 2027-11-30.

Patient Population: Adults aged 18-65 with peripheral nerve injuries (median/ulnar nerve), post-surgical repair. Exclusion criteria include CNS involvement, pregnancy, cardiac pacemakers/arrhythmias, epilepsy. Sample size: 26 estimated.

Target Mechanism: EMG-triggered electrical stimulation targets extensor muscles (EDC, ECRL/B, ECU) to restore muscle weakness from immobilization. Stimulation parameters: 60 Hz, 300 µS pulse width, 0.5s ramp, 10s contraction/30s rest cycle, 12 sessions over 4 weeks starting week 5 post-surgery.

Evidence Sources Retrieved: (1) ClinicalTrials.gov protocol NCT07532499 - trial design only; (2) PMC9028466 - EMG-triggered multichannel FES in stroke patients showing higher gains in FMA-AS vs cNMES; (3) Frontiers in Neurology 2023 review on ES for PNI - clinical studies show ES enhances axon growth and sensorimotor recovery; (4) PMC11962904 - systematic review showing motor outcomes (MMT) most frequently reported after PNI; (5) PMC3746316 - review on peripheral nerve surgery outcomes including MMT, grip/pinch strength, MHQ.

Evidence Role Assessment: PMC9028466 - indirect_direction (stroke vs nerve repair, different pathology but EMG-triggered ES mechanism similar); Frontiers review - indirect_direction (general ES efficacy for PNI); PMC11962904 - mechanism_background (outcome measurement patterns); PMC3746316 - indirect_direction (outcome tools for nerve repair). No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered ES specifically in median/ulnar nerve repair.

Endpoint Interpretation - primary-0 (Manual muscle test): MMT is standard for motor recovery assessment after nerve repair. Evidence suggests ES can enhance motor recovery. Predict EMG+PT group shows greater improvement than PT alone at 12 and 24 weeks. Effect size moderate based on stroke literature extrapolation.

Endpoint Interpretation - secondary-0 (Grip/pinch strength): Dynamometry is objective measure of functional recovery. ES may reduce muscle atrophy and improve reinnervation. Predict EMG+PT group shows 15-25% greater strength recovery vs PT alone.

Endpoint Interpretation - secondary-1 (MHQ): Patient-reported outcome for hand function. Domains include function, ADL, pain, work, aesthetics, satisfaction. Predict EMG+PT group shows clinically meaningful improvement in function and ADL domains; pain domain may show mixed results.

Key Uncertainties: (1) Trial not yet recruiting - no actual outcome data exists; (2) Small sample size (n=26) limits statistical power; (3) Extrapolation from stroke and general PNI literature to specific median/ulnar nerve repair population; (4) Optimal ES parameters not established for this specific indication; (5) Timing of intervention (week 5) relative to nerve regeneration biology.

Safety Analysis: ES generally safe for peripheral nerve rehabilitation. Contraindications (pacemakers, epilepsy) excluded. Expected adverse events: mild skin irritation, discomfort. No serious safety signals anticipated.

Evidence-to-Prediction: Based on mechanistic rationale (ES promotes nerve regeneration, reduces muscle atrophy) and indirect evidence from related populations, EMG-triggered ES is predicted to provide additional benefit over conventional physiotherapy alone for motor recovery outcomes.

Coverage Gaps: No direct RCT evidence for EMG-triggered ES in median/ulnar nerve repair; no published results from this specific trial; limited data on optimal stimulation protocols; no long-term follow-up data available.
